items.stem: Which term matches this description: "A translator that analyses and executes a high-level program one statement at a time, without producing a separate executable"?
options: machine code
interpreter
syntax analysis (parsing)
symbol table
items.answer: interpreter
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of interpreter.

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Interpreted programs usually run more slowly than compiled programs.
Reason (R): An interpreter must translate each statement every time it is executed.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: A. Both true; repeated translation is the reason.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a compiler and an interpreter.
items.answer: A compiler translates the whole program into an executable before running it (fast execution, errors reported together, source hidden); an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time (no executable, stops at the first error, slower, portable source).
items.markingKey: A compiler translates the whole program into an executable before running it (fast execution, errors reported together, source hidden); an interpreter translates and runs one statement at a time (no executable, stops at the first error, slower, portable source). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: A student claims: "Interpreted languages cannot be compiled." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Being interpreted is a property of an implementation, not the language; Python, for example, can be compiled to bytecode or to machine code with tools.
items.markingKey: Being interpreted is a property of an implementation, not the language; Python, for example, can be compiled to bytecode or to machine code with tools. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Recommend a type of translator for a scientific simulation run thousands of times, and justify your choice.
items.answer: compiler: translation cost is paid once and optimised code runs fastest each time.
items.markingKey: 1 mark for compiler; 1-2 marks for justification: translation cost is paid once and optimised code runs fastest each time.

items.stem:
Case study context: Lumen Library, a city library service in Lisbon, offers public Wi-Fi, an online catalogue and e-book lending, and runs its servers in a small on-site data room.
(a) With the help of a specific example, explain why a compiler can report all the syntax errors in a program at once. Refer to Lumen Library in your answer. [3]
(b) Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Developers should always use a compiled language for commercial software." Refer to Lumen Library in your answer. [3]
items.answer: (a) It analyses the entire source code before any of it is executed, so it can continue checking after the first error and list every error with its line number. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (b) Compiled languages suit performance-critical or distributed binaries; many commercial systems successfully use interpreted or bytecode languages.
items.markingKey: (a) [3 marks] Award marks for: It analyses the entire source code before any of it is executed, so it can continue checking after the first error and list every error with its line number. (A specific, correct example that illustrates this is required for full marks.) (one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.) (b) [3 marks] Arguments for: faster execution and source code protection; no interpreter needed by customers. Arguments against: must compile separately for each platform; slower development cycle; JIT-compiled and interpreted languages (Java, Python, JavaScript) are fast enough for most apps. Supported judgement: Compiled languages suit performance-critical or distributed binaries; many commercial systems successfully use interpreted or bytecode languages. items.stem: Which of the following best describes "source code"?
options: The program as written by the programmer in a high-level language
The stage in which the token stream is checked against the grammar of the language and a parse/abstract syntax tree is built
The machine-code output of a compiler, which may need linking before it can run
A meaningful unit of source code, such as a keyword, identifier, operator, literal or punctuation symbol
items.answer: The program as written by the programmer in a high-level language
items.markingKey: A. "source code" is the program as written by the programmer in a high-level language.

items.stem: A compiled executable built for an x86 Windows PC will…
options: automatically recompile itself
run faster on an interpreter
run on any processor
not run directly on an ARM-based phone
items.answer: not run directly on an ARM-based phone
items.markingKey: D. Machine code is specific to an instruction set and OS.

items.stem: Briefly explain why a compiled program usually runs faster than the same program interpreted.
items.answer: Translation is done once in advance and the compiler can optimise the whole program, so at run time the CPU executes machine code directly, whereas an interpreter must analyse each statement every time it is executed (e.g. inside loops).
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Translation is done once in advance and the compiler can optimise the whole program, so at run time the CPU executes machine code directly, whereas an interpreter must analyse each statement every time it is executed (e.g. inside loops). (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why a compiler can report all the syntax errors in a program at once.
items.answer: It analyses the entire source code before any of it is executed, so it can continue checking after the first error and list every error with its line number.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It analyses the entire source code before any of it is executed, so it can continue checking after the first error and list every error with its line number. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Assembly language must be translated before it can be executed.
Reason (R): Assembly programs are usually longer than equivalent high-level programs.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: B. Both true, but program length is not the reason; the CPU can only execute machine code.

items.stem: Explain the difference between an assembler and a compiler.
items.answer: An assembler translates low-level assembly mnemonics into machine code largely one-to-one; a compiler translates high-level statements, each of which may become many machine instructions.
items.markingKey: An assembler translates low-level assembly mnemonics into machine code largely one-to-one; a compiler translates high-level statements, each of which may become many machine instructions. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

The numbered program below contains syntax error(s).

2  x = (8 + 2

items.stem: Compiling a program takes 45 s and the executable then runs in 1 s. Interpreting the same program takes 10 s per run. Calculate the total time for 50 runs with each approach and the number of runs after which compiling becomes faster.
items.answer: Compiled 95 s, interpreted 500 s; compiling is faster after more than 5 runs (i.e. from run 6)
items.markingKey: Compiled = 45 + 1×50 = 95 (A1); interpreted = 10×50 = 500 (A1); break-even 45 + 1n = 10n → n = 5 (M1 A1).

items.stem: A team in Bangalore is building a data-analysis tool that must run on Windows, macOS and Linux and be updated weekly. Compare compiling, interpreting and using bytecode with a virtual machine for this product, and recommend an approach.
items.answer: Compiled: fastest, source hidden, but three builds per release and testing on each platform. Interpreted: one source runs everywhere with the interpreter installed, quick updates, slower, source visible. Bytecode/VM (Java/JVM, Python): compile once to platform-independent bytecode, run on any VM, JIT gives near-native speed. Recommend bytecode/VM: portability with good performance and weekly updates.
items.markingKey: Compiled: fastest, source hidden, but three builds per release and testing on each platform. Interpreted: one source runs everywhere with the interpreter installed, quick updates, slower, source visible. Bytecode/VM (Java/JVM, Python): compile once to platform-independent bytecode, run on any VM, JIT gives near-native speed. Recommend bytecode/VM: portability with good performance and weekly updates.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The first stage of compilation, in which the source code is broken into tokens and whitespace and comments are removed"?
options: hot spot
lexical analysis
ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation
token
items.answer: lexical analysis
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of lexical analysis.

items.stem: Distinguish between lexical analysis and syntax analysis.
items.answer: Lexical analysis converts characters into tokens and spots invalid symbols; syntax analysis checks that the sequence of tokens follows the grammar rules and builds a parse tree.
items.markingKey: Lexical analysis converts characters into tokens and spots invalid symbols; syntax analysis checks that the sequence of tokens follows the grammar rules and builds a parse tree. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): Syntax analysis detects the use of an undeclared variable.
Reason (R): Syntax analysis builds a parse tree from the tokens.
Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true but R is false.
A is false but R is true.
items.answer: A is false but R is true.
items.markingKey: D. A false – undeclared variables are found in semantic analysis; R true.

items.stem: A student claims: "Lexical analysis checks whether the program is grammatically correct." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.

items.markingKey: The lexer only splits the code into tokens; grammar checking is done in syntax analysis. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Describe what happens at each stage of compilation (lexical analysis, syntax analysis, semantic analysis, optimisation, code generation) when the statement total = price * 3 + tax is compiled.
items.answer: Lexical: tokens total (identifier), = (operator), price (identifier), * (operator), 3 (integer literal), + (operator), tax (identifier); symbol-table entries. Syntax: tokens checked against assignment-expression grammar, parse tree built with * before +. Semantic: total, price, tax declared and types compatible. Optimisation: e.g. keep price in a register, constant folding if possible. Code generation: machine code such as LOAD price; MUL #3; ADD tax; STORE total.
items.markingKey: Lexical: tokens total (identifier), = (operator), price (identifier), * (operator), 3 (integer literal), + (operator), tax (identifier); symbol-table entries. Syntax: tokens checked against assignment-expression grammar, parse tree built with * before +. Semantic: total, price, tax declared and types compatible. Optimisation: e.g. keep price in a register, constant folding if possible. Code generation: machine code such as LOAD price; MUL #3; ADD tax; STORE total.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "syntax analysis (parsing)"?
options: An intermediate, platform-independent instruction set produced by compiling source code, designed to be executed by a virtual machine
A data structure built by the compiler that records each identifier with its type, scope and memory location
The stage in which the token stream is checked against the grammar of the language and a parse/abstract syntax tree is built
Transforming the program so that it runs faster or uses less memory without changing its behaviour, e.g. constant folding or removing dead code
items.answer: The stage in which the token stream is checked against the grammar of the language and a parse/abstract syntax tree is built

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "semantic analysis".

items.stem: Briefly explain why the compiler builds a symbol table.
items.answer: Later stages need to know each identifier's type, scope and address – to check declarations and type compatibility (semantic analysis) and to generate the correct memory references (code generation).

items.stem: Explain why lexical analysis happens before syntax analysis.
items.answer: The parser works on tokens; the lexer first groups characters into tokens (identifiers, keywords, numbers), so the grammar can be checked on these meaningful units rather than individual characters.

items.stem: "A virtual machine is the same as an emulator for a games console." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A process VM like the JVM runs an abstract bytecode designed for portability, not a copy of real hardware (though both are forms of virtualisation).

LOAD d
MUL
LOAD a
LOAD b

SUB
State the value left on the stack and the maximum stack depth reached.
items.answer: -2; maximum depth 3

items.stem:

items.answer: (a) The virtual machine that runs Java bytecode (.class files) on any platform (b) JIT compiles bytecode to native code during execution, focusing on hot spots and using run-time information; AOT compiles everything before the program runs, giving fast start-up but no run-time profiling. items.stem: A mobile app developer must choose between distributing native machine code for each phone processor and distributing bytecode run by a VM with JIT compilation. Discuss the implications for performance, portability, start-up time, security and battery life.
items.answer: Native: fastest start-up and execution, less memory, but one build per CPU/OS and harder sandboxing. Bytecode + VM: one build for all devices, verification/sandbox, JIT optimises hot code using run-time profiles, but warm-up delay and JIT work use battery and memory. Many platforms (Android ART) combine AOT at install with JIT – a balanced answer with a justified recommendation.
items.markingKey: Native: fastest start-up and execution, less memory, but one build per CPU/OS and harder sandboxing. Bytecode + VM: one build for all devices, verification/sandbox, JIT optimises hot code using run-time profiles, but warm-up delay and JIT work use battery and memory. Many platforms (Android ART) combine AOT at install with JIT – a balanced answer with a justified recommendation.

items.stem: Why does a JIT compiler not compile every method immediately?
options: Compiling takes time, so only frequently executed (hot) code is worth compiling
JIT compilers cannot compile loops
Bytecode cannot be compiled
It would use too little memory
items.answer: Compiling takes time, so only frequently executed (hot) code is worth compiling
items.markingKey: A. Compilation cost must be repaid by faster repeated execution.

items.stem: Distinguish between JIT compilation and ahead-of-time compilation.
items.answer: JIT compiles bytecode to native code during execution, focusing on hot spots and using run-time information; AOT compiles everything before the program runs, giving fast start-up but no run-time profiling.
items.markingKey: JIT compiles bytecode to native code during execution, focusing on hot spots and using run-time information; AOT compiles everything before the program runs, giving fast start-up but no run-time profiling. items.answer: The VM must load, verify the bytecode and initially interpret it; JIT compilation of hot spots also takes time, so peak speed is reached only after warm-up.

items.stem: A method takes 10 µs per call when interpreted by a VM and 2 µs when JIT-compiled to native code, but compiling it costs 1000 µs. Calculate the total time for 100 calls with and without JIT compilation, and the minimum number of calls for JIT compilation to pay off.
items.answer: Interpreted 1000 µs; JIT 1200 µs; pays off after more than 125 calls
items.markingKey: Interpreted 10×100 = 1000 (A1); JIT 1000 + 2×100 = 1200 (A1); 1000 = (10 − 2)n → n = 125 (M1 A1). This is why VMs only compile hot spots.

LOAD x
LOAD y
LOAD d
ADD
MUL
LOAD a
MUL
State the value left on the stack and the maximum stack depth reached.
items.answer: 52; maximum depth 3
items.markingKey: Stack after each instruction: 1 | 1 6 | 1 6 7 | 1 13 | 13 | 13 4 | 52. Result 52 (2 marks), maximum depth 3 (1 mark).

Supported judgement: Useful for release builds, but debugging builds usually use little optimisation. Markbands (8 marks): top band: well-balanced discussion with accurate, specific technical detail applied to the context and a justified conclusion; middle band: some balance and correct terminology, conclusion only partly supported; bottom band: descriptive, largely one-sided, little technical detail or application.
